models.best: Inferred from its principle that goods move as gifts that create obligations, so essential supplies pass through networks of mutual duty, and no single agency holds the power to withhold them. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that favours are repaid, so rail, power or banks could be built and run only through the trust of particular families and allies, with no single body to fund or account for large works. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Mauss, The Gift; Sahlins, Stone Age Economics.

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a family farm produces to meet its household's needs, so local food and energy stay near the people who use them, with little call on distant owners. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that production serves consumption rather than profit, so a household without spare labour or capital cannot finance a large rail network or power plant, and such works fall to outside owners. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Chayanov, The Theory of Peasant Economy.

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a central authority collects goods and stores them for release, so grain and other essential supplies can be held in common stores and released in shortage without a private owner setting the terms. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the centre allocates what it collects by rank, so access to essential supplies and to the works that supply them depends on the favour of officials, who answer to the centre rather than to users. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Polanyi, The Great Transformation; Polanyi, Arensberg and Pearson, Trade and Market in the Early Empires.

models.best: Inferred from its principle that owners command labour directly, so they can assign large gangs to one undertaking at once, such as clearing land or running a plantation or mine, and sell the output through trade. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that labour is extracted through ownership of people, so an owner or colonial legislature controls a strategic industry with no check from its workers, who are denied education and property and cannot bargain or leave. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Williams, Capitalism and Slavery.

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a lord protects and governs the land in return for services, so defence, justice and a largely self-supplying manor are kept under one hand. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that peasants owe labour and rent to a lord, so control of the land's output and of local works rests with the lord, and tenants have little means to change the terms. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Bloch, Feudal Society; Capitulare de villis.

models.best: Inferred from its principle that statutes set training, quality and prices, so the trades that supply a town keep set standards of quality and skill. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that masters regulate entry and prices, so newcomers can be kept out of a trade that supplies a town, and prices are set by a closed body rather than by competition. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Boileau, Le Livre des métiers; Epstein, Freedom and Growth.

models.best: Inferred from its principle that the state aims for a trade surplus, so it can keep key trades, credit and colonial supply under national control and steer them toward that aim. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the state regulates production and trade to its own end, so firms outside the favoured trades are restricted and goods are directed by officials rather than by the owners who make them. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Mun, England's Treasure by Forraign Trade; Heckscher, Mercantilism.

models.best: Inferred from its principle that only agriculture creates a net product, so the state has little reason to own factories, banks or transport, and its revenue comes from a single tax on the rent of land. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that only agriculture creates a net product, so manufacturing, transport and power are left to private hands with no state plan, and strategic supplies outside farming may run short when the state cannot direct them. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Quesnay, Tableau économique; Meek, The Economics of Physiocracy.

models.best: Inferred from its principle that competitive markets and private property create wealth, so private owners who must compete for custom are pressed to run energy, rail and banks efficiently. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the state stays out, so a strategic service such as rail or power can fall into a private monopoly where no competitor exists, and the state, having left it alone, has few means to correct its prices or service. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Smith, The Wealth of Nations.

models.best: Inferred from its principle that prices carry knowledge spread across many people, so private owners who must pay their way can judge where energy, rail and banks should expand, without a planner. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: In the case State ownership of banks and growth: two views, the authors set a 'political view' against a 'developmental' one: politicians steer state banks toward allies, producing bad loans and slower growth. Inferred from its principle that state planning and credit expansion distort production, the outcome would fit this model's warning. These are working papers with data that stop in 2007, and a summary of the work calls the finding contested. Source: Andrianova, Demetriades and Shortland, Government ownership of banks, institutions and economic growth (working papers and conference abstracts, 2009 to 2010).

models.best: In the case Japan's national railway (JNR) privatised, a Kobe University paper estimates total factor productivity growth at about 3% a year after privatisation, with roughly 1.6 points attributable to the reform. These figures come from an abstract, not the full paper.
models.worst: In the case Argentina's YPF: privatised, then partly renationalised, it was privatised in the 1990s, and Argentina moved to expropriate Repsol's 51% stake. A CORE paper finds some gains alongside shortfalls. CEPAL's findings are not reported, the CORE and Serrani pieces are articles without figures, and the sources differ in emphasis. Source: CEPAL (UN Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean), report on YPF's renationalisation (2015, abstract); Serrani, Recent transformations in the Argentine oil industry: the YPF case, 1989 to 2012, Revista de Gestión Pública (year not shown); CORE repository paper on the hybrid renationalisation of YPF, 2012 to 2015 (year not shown).

models.best: Inferred from its principle that government spending rises in slumps and falls in booms, so demand for energy, transport and credit stays steady, whoever owns the firms that supply them. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the state steers spending while firms stay with their owners, so public money can flow to firms the state does not run and cannot direct, leaving the supply of strategic goods to those firms' own plans. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Keynes, The General Theory; Beveridge, Social Insurance and Allied Services.

models.best: Inferred from its principle that competitive markets operate inside a legal order that curbs monopoly, so energy, rail and bank firms must compete, and worker representation gives their staff a voice. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that a legal order curbs monopoly, so a large firm in energy, rail or banking can still hold a dominant place if the curbs are weak, and neither owners nor the state need then answer to customers. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Müller-Armack, Wirtschaftslenkung und Marktwirtschaft; Erhard, Wohlstand für Alle.

models.best: Inferred from its principle that universal public services are financed by high taxes and open to everyone, so essential services such as transport and energy can be provided publicly, with strong unions taking part in pay and terms. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that high taxes fund universal services, so a public provider that is slow to change or costly to run can absorb large sums that are then hard to redirect, and national wage bargaining can leave local firms with little say. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Saltsjöbaden Agreement; Esping-Andersen, The Three Worlds of Welfare Capitalism.

models.best: In the case India's takeover of 14 major banks, officials justified the move by national goals such as farming, small industry and exports, and the paper says any gains in equity and efficiency depend on credit reaching agriculture and small industry. The paper's lending results are not reported in these sources, so the case cannot show what happened to credit.
models.worst: In the case State ownership of banks and growth: two views, the authors set a 'political view' against a 'developmental' one: politicians steer state banks toward allies, producing bad loans and slower growth. These are working papers with data that stop in 2007, and a summary of the work calls the finding contested. Source: Andrianova, Demetriades and Shortland, Government ownership of banks, institutions and economic growth (working papers and conference abstracts, 2009 to 2010).

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a tax on the value of land takes land rent for public use, so the rent from natural sites pays for public services without a tax on labour and capital. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that land rent is collected for the public, so public bodies must value strategic sites each year, and a site left in private hands can still be held idle for speculation if the tax is weak. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: George, Progress and Poverty.

models.best: Inferred from its principle that cooperative communities and planned associations replace private profit by example, so energy, transport and credit could be run by members for shared needs. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that communities are built by example and planned by their founders, so a strategic enterprise such as a railway or bank may rest on a few founders' judgment and fail when they leave or when members disagree. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Owen, A New View of Society; Fourier, Le Nouveau Monde industriel.

models.best: Inferred from its principle that mutual credit lets banks lend at cost, so credit for workers and small producers stays cheap, and no owner collects rent on property used for strategic supply. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that free contracts govern exchange, so mutual banks may stay small and local, and a strategic network that needs large capital, such as rail or power, can be left without the funds it needs. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Proudhon, What Is Property?

models.best: Inferred from its principle that members own and control firms and banks, one member one vote, so the users and workers of an energy or rail firm share its surplus and decide its direction. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the surplus is shared between users and workers, so investment in a costly network such as rail or power can be held back when members want their share now, and members' voting may slow decisions to raise capital. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Rochdale Society of Equitable Pioneers; Mondragón cooperatives.

models.best: Inferred from its principle that goods are shared by need within federated communes, so energy, water and transport are provided without wages or a state, by the communes that use them. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that no state and no wages govern production, so a strategic network that spans many communes depends on voluntary agreement, and a dispute among communes may leave supply unsettled. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Kropotkin, The Conquest of Bread.

models.best: Inferred from its principle that trade unions run industry through workers' organisations, so the people who operate a railway or power network decide how it is run and bargain directly over its conditions. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that unions run industry through strikes and, eventually, a general strike, so a strategic service can be halted by a dispute, and a workers' organisation may put its own aims above those of the public it serves. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Founding of the French CGT; Pelloutier, Histoire des Bourses du travail.

models.best: In the case Hamburg buys back its energy grids, voters backed a takeover of the city's grids by 50.9% in a 2013 referendum, despite opposition from most major parties. The electricity distribution network changed hands in early 2014 at an expected price of about 400 million euros, from news and blog summaries that cover events only to about 2017 and say nothing of later performance.
models.worst: In the case India's takeover of 14 major banks, the paper says any gains in equity and efficiency depend on credit reaching agriculture and small industry, and that cross-country research cuts against state ownership. The paper's lending results are not reported in these sources, so the case cannot show what happened to credit. Source: Banerjee, Cole and Duflo, Banking reform in India (2004), a paper hosted by Brookings; Reserve Bank of India annual report (year not shown in the result).

models.best: Inferred from its principle that workers and consumers share control of industry through guild-like councils, so the people who use and run a strategic service take part in its decisions, with the state as one partner among several. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that councils share control with the state as one partner among several, so a strategic service may be slow to act when councils and the state disagree, and a council of workers may protect its own jobs ahead of the needs of users. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Cole, Self-Government in Industry.

models.best: Inferred from its principle that state ownership and central plans set output, prices and investment, so the state can direct labour and capital to energy, rail and heavy industry for rapid industrialisation. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that central plans set output, prices and investment, so a plan that misjudges what energy, rail or credit users need has no price signal to correct it, and shortages can last while labour is directed to the plan's targets. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Kornai, The Socialist System; First Five-Year Plan.

models.best: Inferred from its principle that public ownership works with market prices, so managers who follow prices can run firms in energy, rail and banking, while a central board sets the rules and the investment. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that a central board sets the rules and the investment while managers are meant to follow market prices, so investment in energy, rail or banking may follow the board's choices rather than those prices, and losses may go uncorrected if the board keeps funding them. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Lange and Taylor, On the Economic Theory of Socialism; Yugoslav workers' self-management.

models.best: Inferred from its principle that after the state withers away and classes disappear, distribution follows ability and need rather than price or profit, so the output of energy, rail and credit is shared by need. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the state withers away only after classes disappear, so the period before that leaves a state in charge of energy, rail and banks, with power to decide who receives what, and the timing of the withering is left open. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Marx, Critique of the Gotha Programme.

models.best: In the case State ownership of banks and growth: two views, the authors find that state ownership of banks tracked with stronger long-run growth on average, using cross-country data for 1995 to 2007. They concede these correlations may not reflect causation; the working papers' data stop in 2007, and a summary calls the finding contested.
models.worst: In the case State ownership of banks and growth: two views, the authors set out a political view in which politicians steer state banks toward allies, producing bad loans and slower growth. These are working papers with data that stop in 2007, and a summary calls the finding contested. Source: Andrianova, Demetriades and Shortland, Government ownership of banks, institutions and economic growth (working papers and conference abstracts, 2009 to 2010).

models.best: Inferred from its principle that workers' and consumers' councils plan through repeated proposals, so energy, rail and banking are run by the people who use them, with neither markets nor central planners allocating. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that councils plan by repeated proposals, so a strategic service may be slow to decide and costly to run, and jobs balanced in complexity may leave a network short-staffed while a plan is agreed. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Albert and Hahnel, Looking Forward.

models.best: Inferred from its principle that employers and unions are organised into state-controlled corporations, so the state can direct energy, transport and credit toward national goals through one plan for each sector. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: In the case Italy's IRI state holding, 1933 to 2002, IRI was set up in 1933 to rescue lenders whose firms were failing, made permanent in 1937, and at its peak controlled roughly 1,000 subsidiaries. The state stopped covering its debt in the early 1990s, and it was wound up in 2002. These dates are thin: they come from profiles and a book listing, and one profile still lists IRI as active. Source: Company history profiles of Istituto per la Ricostruzione Industriale (Funding Universe; year not shown in the results); bookseller listing for Storia dell'IRI volume 4, Crisi e privatizzazione, covering 1990 to 2002.

models.best: Inferred from its principle that interest is prohibited and finance shares profit and risk, so banks that back firms share their gains and losses, and trust underpins the contracts that move credit. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that finance shares profit and risk, so a bank's lending depends on the honesty of its partners, and a strategic supplier that relies on trust rather than collateral may be short of credit when that trust breaks down. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Chapra, Towards a Just Monetary System; Founding of the Mit Ghamr savings bank.

models.best: Inferred from its principle that economic life serves well-being, so energy and transport are kept small-scale and local, which keeps control close to the people who use them. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that production is small-scale and local, so a large strategic network such as a national rail line or grid may be left unbuilt or split into local pieces that do not connect. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Schumacher, Buddhist Economics; Schumacher, Small Is Beautiful.

models.best: Inferred from its principle that property is widely held and enterprise is small, so energy, transport and credit stay in many small hands, and decisions rest with the smallest competent body. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the smallest competent body decides, so a large strategic network that needs one operator, such as a rail line or grid, may be split into small units that do not connect, and small owners may lack the capital to build it. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Leo XIII, Rerum Novarum; Belloc, The Servile State.

models.best: Inferred from its principle that economic activity stays within planetary limits, so strategic supplies such as energy and water are planned against those limits, and a social floor reaches everyone. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that there is no growth imperative, so investment in new energy, rail or bank capacity may be held back, and the social floor depends on who owns and runs those services. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Daly, Steady-State Economics; Raworth, Doughnut Economics.

models.best: Inferred from its principle that an unconditional income is paid for by taxes on land and natural resources, so rent from energy sites and other resources pays a share to every citizen. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that resource rent pays for the income, so the amount depends on how much rent is collected, and public bodies must value resources such as energy sites every year to set it. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Paine, Agrarian Justice; Van Parijs, Real Freedom for All.

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a government which issues its own currency can fund full employment, so strategic investment in energy, rail and banks need not be borrowed from private lenders, with inflation as the real limit. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that inflation is the real limit, so a state that funds strategic industries by issuing currency can push prices up in shortage, and the state's own firms and banks may have to carry that inflation risk. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Kelton, The Deficit Myth.

models.best: Inferred from its principle that communities who share a resource govern it with rules they design, monitor and enforce, so shared strategic resources such as water, grazing or a local grid can be run by their users. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that community rules sit within wider institutions, so a community's control of a shared network depends on those institutions recognising it, and a network too large for its users may fall to the state or to a private owner. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Ostrom, Governing the Commons.

compromise.summary: A mixed design for strategic industries: keep public ownership of grids, rail and bank credit where markets do not supply them, run at arm's length from ministers with published lending and investment rules, and sell holdings only by open competition, with a review date for each public holding.
compromise.details: Keeps: Developmental state's directed credit (India's takeover of 14 major banks, whose lending results are not reported); Fabian socialism's municipal ownership (Hamburg buys back its energy grids); Monetarist neoliberalism's productivity gains (Japan's national railway (JNR) privatised, an abstract's estimate). Blocks: political lending, guarded by published loan rules (State ownership of banks and growth: two views, a contested finding); a sale later reversed, guarded by fixed sale terms (Argentina's YPF: privatised, then partly renationalised); a state holding kept past its purpose, guarded by five-yearly review (Italy's IRI state holding, 1933 to 2002, with thin dates). Test: over ten years, credit to farming and small firms, loan losses, productivity and debt, public against private firms in one sector. Source: Banerjee, Cole and Duflo (2004); Andrianova, Demetriades and Shortland (2009 to 2010); Kobe University repository paper (2005); Energy Transition website articles (2013 and 2014); Company history profiles of Istituto per la Ricostruzione Industriale; CEPAL report on YPF's renationalisation (2015); Serrani (year not shown); CORE repository paper (year not shown).
